desc:
Place n pieces on an n × n board. Each piece threatens everything a queen threatens (its row, its column, both diagonals) and everything a knight threatens (squares that are 1 row and 2 columns, or 2 rows and 1 column, away). No piece may threaten another.

Return the number of different placements of the n pieces. Pieces on a threatened line do not shield each other, and all pieces look the same.

n = 1   →  1
n = 4   →  0
n = 10  →  4
hints: Two pieces may not share a row, so a valid placement has exactly one piece per row (n pieces, n rows). Search row by row.
As in N-Queens, mark columns and both diagonals as taken. The extra knight rule only links pieces in rows that are one or two apart.
When choosing a column in row r, also forbid a ± 2 where a is the column used in row r - 1, and b ± 1 where b is the column used in row r - 2. With bitmasks this is two shifts per neighbour row.
editorial: Start from the N-Queens backtracking: one piece per row, columns tried from a free-mask, diagonals tracked with shifted masks. The knight rule adds a local restriction, because a knight move changes the row by 1 or 2. A piece in row r - 1 at column a forbids columns a - 2 and a + 2 in row r, and a piece in row r - 2 at column b forbids b - 1 and b + 1. Only the last two placed columns matter, so pass them down the recursion.

The extra restriction prunes the tree strongly, which is why small boards have zero solutions and even n = 12 stays cheap. Counting is exhaustive: the number of leaves reached at depth n is the answer (4 for n = 10).
